notes: No political parties in Tonga in 1970. Ruling slot 23 holds the House of Tupou (MD puts it in slot 0, but the ruling slot must hold the regime); slot 0 gets the Privy Council instead. Slots 1/2 are the nobles' and people's representatives in the Legislative Assembly; slot 13 the Tu'ipelehake government; slot 22 the Tonga Defence Services.

0.name: Fakataha Tokoni
0.text:
The Privy Council is the king's executive council, made up of the cabinet ministers and the governors of Ha'apai and Vava'u, all appointed by and answerable to Taufa'ahau Tupou IV rather than to the Legislative Assembly. It issues ordinances, hears final appeals in land and title cases and is the real seat of government in Nuku'alofa. With British protection set to end in June 1970, it prepares to take charge of foreign affairs.

The council stands for royal government aligned with Britain, Australia, New Zealand and the United States: firm order, anti-communism, Western aid and investment. It sees parliamentary reform as premature. Its leverage is total: it controls appointments, land administration and the purse.

1.name: Fakafofonga 'o e Hou'eiki Nōpele
1.text:
The Nobles' Representatives are the seven members of the Legislative Assembly chosen by and from the thirty-three hereditary nobles of Tonga. Together with the king's ministers they hold a permanent majority over the seven elected People's Representatives, and their hereditary estates cover much of the kingdom's land, on which commoners hold allotments by law.

The nobles defend the 1875 constitution, hereditary land tenure and the hierarchy that binds chief and commoner. They welcome Western development money but oppose any move toward one person, one vote or ministerial responsibility to the Assembly. Their leverage lies in land, titles and privileged access to the king.

2.name: Fakafofonga 'o e Kakai
2.text:
The People's Representatives are the seven commoner members of the Legislative Assembly, elected by adult Tongans every three years. Without parties, they stand as individuals, often teachers, pastors or civil servants, and in the Assembly they are outnumbered by the nobles' members and the king's ministers.

Some of them are beginning to voice commoner grievances: the shortage of land allotments for a growing population, the privileges of noble estates, government spending and the lack of ministerial accountability. They are loyal to the crown and pro-Western, but favour gradual constitutional reform and a stronger Assembly. Their leverage lies in popular legitimacy and in a rising, educated commoner class.

3.name: Kau Ngāue
3.text:
Kau Ngāue is the voice of Tonga's small wage-earning class: dock hands at the Nuku'alofa wharf, hotel and construction workers, government labourers and the growing number of Tongans who go to New Zealand on temporary work permits. Tonga has no trade unions, so grievances are aired in churches, kava circles and letters home.

Its aims are moderate: fair wages, safety at work, housing in the capital and protection for workers abroad, with the New Zealand Labour Party as a distant model. It is loyal to the crown and anti-communist, but wants the government to recognise labour as a constituency. Its leverage grows with every remittance sent home.

4.name: Kalapu Kulokula
4.text:
Kalapu Kulokula is a handful of young men in Nuku'alofa's kava clubs who have come across Marxist books and Soviet broadcasts while working or studying abroad. Tonga has no communist party and the churches and police would quickly suppress one; the group exists as private talk, a few smuggled pamphlets and contacts with left-wing unionists in Auckland and Sydney.

Its members describe the nobles as a landlord class and the king's government as a monarchy propped up by Britain and Western missions. They call for the abolition of hereditary estates, land to the people and friendship with the socialist countries. Their influence is negligible, but they cast the commoners' land hunger in revolutionary terms.

5.name: To'utupu Fo'ou
5.text:
To'utupu Fo'ou is the mood of Tongan students at the University of the South Pacific in Suva, at colleges in New Zealand and Australia, and at Tupou College and Tonga High School at home. They have watched campus protests against the Vietnam War and colonialism, and they return to a kingdom where nobles rule and dissent is discouraged.

They want free expression, a fully elected parliament, land reform and an end to deference to chiefs and clergy, and they sympathise with Third World liberation movements. They have no organisation beyond student clubs and church youth fellowships. Their leverage is their education: the kingdom needs them to staff its ministries.

6.name: Tonga Motu'a
6.text:
Tonga Motu'a gathers elderly chiefs, ceremonial attendants and village elders who fear that the king's modernising programme of hotels, tourism, roads and new schools is eroding the Tongan way. They distrust foreign advisers, tourists and the rapid spread of the Mormon mission and other new churches.

They want custom and rank honoured above money, foreign influence kept at arm's length, and land and titles shielded from any reform. Their outlook is hostile to Western consumer culture and to the open economy the government courts, though not to the monarchy itself. They have no organisation; their leverage lies in ceremony, kinship and the respect still owed to age and rank.

7.name: Pule Mālohi
7.text:
Pule Mālohi is the conviction, found among some palace officials and younger nobles, that Tonga should use the end of British protection to chart its own course. They resent dependence on British, Australian and New Zealand aid and are open to approaches from any power, including the Soviet Union, that offers fishing deals, money or prestige.

They favour a stronger executive answerable only to the crown, state control of trade and development projects, and firm limits on the press and the Assembly. They see Western conditions on aid as interference. They have no organisation of their own; their leverage depends on the king's own interest in widening Tonga's circle of foreign friends.

8.name: Halqat Ahl al-Bayt
8.text:
Halqat Ahl al-Bayt is a handful of Muslim seamen and Indo-Fijian traders who call at Nuku'alofa and occasionally meet for prayer; a few follow Shia teaching learned from Khoja communities in East Africa and India. Tonga has no mosque, no settled Muslim community and a constitution that gives the Christian Sabbath the force of law.

The circle shares the reformist Shia outlook associated with Musa al-Sadr in Lebanon: faith joined to social justice, education and the dignity of the poor, pursued within existing law. It has no political ambitions in the kingdom. Its only relevance lies in the threads of contact it maintains with the wider Muslim world.

9.name: Ansar al-Najaf
9.text:
Ansar al-Najaf is the name a few transient Shia believers give to their loyalty to Ayatollah Ruhollah Khomeini, the exiled Iranian cleric whose lectures on Islamic government circulate from Najaf. In Tonga they are almost invisible: sailors and labourers passing through the port with recordings and pamphlets from the Gulf.

They hold that legitimate rule belongs to the Islamic jurist, condemn both American and Soviet power, and regard monarchies allied to the West as illegitimate. They have no Tongan followers. Any influence would depend on a revolution in the Muslim heartlands that gives their cause money, prestige and a state to back it.

10.name: Rabitat al-'Alam al-Islami
10.text:
The Muslim World League, founded in Mecca in 1962 under Saudi royal patronage, funds mosques, literature and scholarships for Muslim communities worldwide and reaches the South Pacific through Fiji. In Tonga it has no presence beyond the occasional pamphlet or letter reaching a Muslim visitor or curious reader.

The League preaches a Saudi-sponsored orthodoxy that respects pious monarchs, rejects communism and secular nationalism, and aligns with the West against Soviet influence. It builds institutions rather than parties and works with governments, not against them. Its leverage is money: any Muslim community that took root in the kingdom would look to it first for support.

11.name: Da'wat al-Khilafa
11.text:
Da'wat al-Khilafa is the idea of a restored caliphate as spread by Hizb ut-Tahrir pamphlets that reach a few Muslim students at universities in Australia, New Zealand and Fiji. Tongan contact with it is limited to the rare student abroad who meets its activists and brings their literature home.

The circle rejects kingship, democracy and nationalism alike as man-made systems, and calls for a single Islamic state under one caliph that would end both Western and Soviet domination. It is secretive and contemptuous of established Muslim leaders. In a devout Christian monarchy it has no leverage beyond the curiosity of a few disaffected young people.

12.name: Fiji Muslim League
12.text:
The Fiji Muslim League, founded in 1926 by Indo-Fijian Muslims, runs mosques, schools and welfare work across Fiji and is the leading Muslim body in the South Pacific. Its members trade with Tonga and occasionally work in Nuku'alofa, and it is the natural point of contact for anyone in the kingdom drawn to Islam.

The League combines religious education with community uplift and peaceful participation in politics, influenced by the revivalist currents of South Asian Islam. It is anti-communist and works within the institutions of the state. In Tonga it has no presence beyond individual contacts; its leverage lies in Fiji, where Indo-Fijians now outnumber indigenous Fijians.

13.name: Pule'anga Tonga
13.text:
The Government of Tonga, led since 1965 by Prime Minister Prince Fatafehi Tu'ipelehake, the king's younger brother, runs the kingdom's ministries, development plans and state bodies such as the Copra Board. Its officials, many trained in New Zealand, Australia and Britain, pursue the king's vision of modernisation through the first national development plan.

The administration is pragmatic and non-ideological: roads, wharves, schools, health services, tourism and new export crops, funded by whichever donor will pay. It prefers expert decision-making to public debate and treats the Assembly as a body to be consulted, not obeyed. Its leverage lies in controlling budgets, jobs and the flow of aid.

14.name: Siasi Uēsiliana Tau'atāina 'o Tonga
14.text:
The Free Wesleyan Church of Tonga, reunited from rival Methodist bodies under Queen Sālote in 1924, is the kingdom's largest church, and the monarch is its head. Its chapels stand in every village, its colleges such as Tupou College educate much of the elite, and its ministers sit close to the nobles and the palace.

The church upholds Sunday observance, which the constitution enshrines, family discipline, loyalty to the crown and the moral order of chief and commoner. It is anti-communist and pro-Western but wary of secular change and of rival missions. Its leverage is enormous: it shapes opinion, mobilises congregations and lends sacred legitimacy to the monarchy.

15.name: Burns Philp
15.text:
Burns Philp, the Australian shipping and trading house, has long dominated Tonga's import trade and copra buying through its stores and agencies in Nuku'alofa, Ha'apai and Vava'u. Its managers, together with a few European and part-Tongan merchant families, form the core of the kingdom's commercial elite and deal directly with ministers and nobles.

The firm stands for secure trade, favourable shipping terms and minimal government competition in commerce. It looks to Australia and New Zealand as markets and resists state marketing bodies encroaching on its business. Its leverage lies in credit and supply: villages and the government alike depend on the goods its ships carry.

16.name: Morris Hedstrom
16.text:
Morris Hedstrom, the Fiji-based trading company, operates stores and buying agencies in Tonga and represents the more competitive edge of the kingdom's commerce. Around it gather smaller Tongan shopkeepers and returned migrants opening businesses with savings earned in New Zealand.

This milieu wants open markets, freedom to trade without official controls on copra and imports, low duties and easier leasing of land for business. It is pro-Western and impatient with noble privilege where it blocks enterprise. Its leverage lies in the growing weight of private trade and remittances in an economy that the government and the old merchant houses can no longer fully control.

17.name: Fonua mo e Tahi
17.text:
Fonua mo e Tahi gathers village elders, fishermen and church groups worried about the pressure on Tonga's land and reefs. A growing population leaves too few allotments, coconut groves are ageing, mangroves are cleared around the Fanga'uta lagoon and reef fish grow scarce near Nuku'alofa. The concern is voiced at village meetings rather than through any organisation.

It wants land kept in Tongan hands, reefs and lagoons protected from overfishing and pollution, and development that respects the islands' limits. It is suspicious of foreign land deals and resort schemes. Its leverage lies in the constitutional ban on selling land and in the reverence for fonua that runs through Tongan culture.

18.name: Langafonua 'a Fafine Tonga
18.text:
Langafonua, the women's association founded by Queen Sālote in 1953, links village women's groups across Tongatapu, Ha'apai and Vava'u. It began by reviving tapa-making, mat-weaving and handicrafts and now also promotes hygiene, nutrition, home gardens and small earnings for families.

Its outlook is communal and developmental rather than partisan: better village living conditions, women's incomes, preservation of Tongan crafts and cooperation between villages. It is close to the royal family and neutral in world affairs. Its leverage comes from organisation: it reaches nearly every household and delivers what the ministries cannot.

19.name: Taulanga Kulokula
19.text:
Taulanga Kulokula is a tiny circle of dock workers and seamen at the Nuku'alofa wharf who have met Maoist ideas in foreign ports and through the pro-Beijing Communist Party of New Zealand. They read Mao Zedong's Quotations in English and talk of a peasant revolution in a kingdom of smallholders.

They denounce the nobles as feudal landlords and Western aid as neocolonialism, call for land to be redistributed to those who till it and for village self-reliance, and reject the Soviet Union as revisionist. They have no organisation and no newspaper, and the police would act quickly against them. Their importance lies only in the land question they exploit.

20.name: Tonga ma'a Tonga
20.text:
Tonga ma'a Tonga voices the pride of a kingdom that was never colonised and is about to regain full sovereignty. Its adherents, commoners and minor chiefs alike, resent the influence of European and part-European merchants, foreign missions and the British agent, and cherish the constitutional rule that Tongan land may never be sold to foreigners.

They want Tongans to own every business and hold every post of consequence, restrictions on foreign traders and missionaries, and a foreign policy that bows to no one. They are loyal to the crown and devoutly Christian, but quick to suspect outsiders. Their leverage lies in national pride, which the end of British protection only strengthens.

21.name: Toa 'o Tonga
21.text:
Toa 'o Tonga draws on the memory of the warrior chiefs who fought the civil wars of the early nineteenth century before George Tupou I united the islands. It is the outlook of young men in the Defence Services and in noble households who believe the kingdom needs martial discipline and absolute obedience to rank.

They want the Assembly reduced to a formality, dissenters punished, foreign ideas excluded and the nation organised around king, chiefs and warrior virtue. They admire strong-arm order wherever it appears. They have no organisation or recognised leader, and the king's own modernising instincts keep them at the margins.

22.name: Tonga Defence Services
22.text:
The Tonga Defence Services are the kingdom's small armed force, including the royal guard, with a tradition reaching back to the Tongan troops who served alongside New Zealand forces in the Second World War. They answer directly to the king, and their officers come largely from noble and well-connected families.

The force is loyal, ceremonial and politically silent, but it is the only armed institution besides the police. Its officers value hierarchy, discipline and the security of the throne, and look to New Zealand and Britain for training. Its leverage would matter only in a crisis that threatened the monarchy or public order in Nuku'alofa.

23.name: House of Tupou
23.text:
The House of Tupou has ruled Tonga since George Tupou I unified the islands and granted the constitution of 1875. King Taufa'ahau Tupou IV, who succeeded his mother Queen Sālote in 1965 and was crowned in 1967, governs with his brother Prince Fatafehi Tu'ipelehake as prime minister and the Privy Council as his executive. British protection is set to end in June 1970.

The dynasty stands for royal authority, Christian order, hereditary land tenure and cautious modernisation. Tupou IV pursues development, education, tourism and new partners while keeping close ties with Britain and the Commonwealth. Its leverage is near absolute: it appoints the government, controls the nobility and commands deep popular loyalty.
